one_liner: SIMD array-mode log/exp for float buffers, 9-19x faster than std::logf/std::expf via AVX2/AVX-512.
what_it_does: fmath exposes two array functions, fmath_logf_v and fmath_expf_v, that compute dst[i] = log(src[i]) or exp(src[i]) over a whole float array in one call, replacing a per-element loop of std::logf/std::expf. It is not a drop-in for scalar std::logf/std::expf: call sites must build contiguous src/dst float buffers and call the array function instead of invoking std:: per element. CPU dispatch between the AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels happens once via fmath_init(), exposed as global function pointers fmath_logf_v/fmath_expf_v (also wrapped in a fmath:: C++ namespace).
how_it_is_fast: The log/exp kernels are not written as C++ that the compiler auto-vectorizes; they are generated ahead of time as raw x86 machine code by a Python script (src/gen_fmath.py) using the bundled s_xbyak assembler-generation library, emitting GAS (src/fmath.S) or MASM (src/fmath.asm) that gets assembled into libfmath. This gives hand-tuned SIMD kernels that process 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX-512) floats per instruction using a polynomial/lookup-table approximation (table size tunable via LOG_L), amortizing per-call overhead across the whole array in one pass. fmath_init(), run via a GCC constructor attribute or an MSVC CRT init-section hook before main(), auto-selects the AVX-512 kernel when the CPU supports AVX512F+DQ, else falls back to the AVX2 baseline.
when_to_use: Hot loops applying std::logf/std::expf over float arrays with n >= 16 that can be laid out as contiguous src/dst buffers
x86-64 targets guaranteeing AVX2; extra speedup available automatically on AVX-512F+DQ Xeons/desktops
Single-precision-only workloads (audio, ML feature transforms, scientific arrays) where a fast SIMD approximation's accuracy is acceptable
Throughput-bound batch processing rather than single-call latency, e.g. bulk activation functions or vectorized transforms
when_not_to_use: Calls with n < 16 elements — the readme explicitly states fmath's array functions are slower than std:: there
Double precision needed — fmath.h declares only float (logf/expf) variants, no logd/expd in this version
Scalar call sites that can't be restructured into array form, since the API has no single-value entry point of its own
Platforms without AVX2 (older x86-64 chips, ARM/aarch64) — AVX2 is a hard minimum, not degraded gracefully further
Projects wanting a small header-only drop-in — this ships as generated assembly built into a static lib, not header-only, despite include/fmath.h existing

integration.dependencies: bundled s_xbyak.py (codegen) and xbyak_util.h (runtime CPU feature detection); Python 3 to (re)generate src/fmath.S/.asm; no external runtime deps once built
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (Makefile builds with -std=c++20, mk.bat with /std:c++20); GCC/Clang on Linux or MSVC cl on Windows
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 required minimum; auto-upgrades to AVX-512F+DQ kernels if detected at startup; no ARM/aarch64 support documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the AVX2-vs-AVX-512 dispatch (global function pointers) is written once via a constructor/CRT-init hook before main(), so concurrent calls into fmath_logf_v/fmath_expf_v on disjoint buffers appear safe, but the project makes no explicit thread-safety claim

gotchas: Dispatch can be pinned to the AVX2 kernel with the FMATH_CPU=avx2 environment variable, and the AVX-512 log variant switched to the lower-max-error 'tq' form with FMATH_LOG=tq
No LICENSE file exists in the repo (GitHub's detector reports license: null); BSD-3-Clause is only stated in readme.md and the fmath.h header comment

This is a rewrite that is explicitly not backward compatible with the older single-header fmath.hpp/Xbyak-JIT version; a since-fixed NaN bug (exp(89.0f), issue #14) was reported and patched against that old version, not this one
Benchmark numbers are cycles-per-32-elements on specific CPUs; the readme does not state which compiler or flags produced them
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among siblings, VDT and SLEEF also cover exp/log but at per-call scalar latency (VDT: ~2.8-12.8x vs libm) or double precision; fmath is narrower (float32 logf/expf only, array-mode only) but shows the largest claimed log/exp speedup (9.4-19.5x) because it measures bulk array throughput on AVX2/AVX-512, not single calls. Pick fmath when you specifically need bulk float32 log/exp over large contiguous arrays on x86-64 and can restructure call sites into array form; pick VDT/SLEEF/FastMath C++ instead for scalar call sites, double precision, or a broader function set (sin/cos/pow, etc.).
verified_claims_summary: On the project's own readme benchmark tables (average CPU cycles per 32 elements), fmath's array-mode logf_v/expf_v beat scalar std::log/std::exp array loops by 15.7x/18.5x on a Linux Xeon w9-3495X (AVX-512), 16.9x/19.5x on a Windows Core i7-1165G7 (AVX-512), and 9.4x/12.9x on a Windows Core i7-1255U without AVX-512; compiler and flags used for these numbers are not stated. The comparison code (test/log_v.cpp, test/exp_v.cpp), which loops std::log/std::exp over the same arrays, is public in the repo.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-31, 244 stars, 36 forks) and BSD-3-Clause per readme/header, but there is no standalone LICENSE file, and this version is a non-backward-compatible rewrite of the older fmath.hpp/Xbyak-JIT API, so old issues and usage examples don't carry over.
